Read `lib/init.mjs` rather than just the README blurb. `npx @opengsd/gsd-loop@latest init` is a preview-then-confirm bootstrap:

**Preflight** — requires `gh` installed and authenticated (`gh --version`, `gh auth status`), then resolves the git root. No git root at all: it offers to create the repo (empty commit → `gh repo create --source . --remote origin --push`). Git root but no GitHub remote: hard error telling you to run `install` instead, add a remote, and rerun. It also dry-runs the skill install and, on an existing repo, runs its doctor to find missing labels and lists successful check-runs on the default branch head so you can pick one.

**Preview** — prints the plan and waits for confirmation (`--dry-run` prints and exits):

- Install or update the five `gsd-loop-*` skills for your chosen agents
- Create whichever `gsd:` labels are missing — `ready`, `blocked`, `approved`, `rework`, `escalated`
- Exclude `.gsd/scheduled_tasks.lock` from the worktree
- Either "require successful check: *name*" or "leave review blocked until a successful CI check exists"

**Apply** — creates the repo if new, installs the skills for real, appends that lock path to `.git/info/exclude`, creates the labels, then creates or updates a GitHub **ruleset** requiring your chosen check on the default branch. If rulesets aren't available for the repo's plan or your permissions, it warns rather than failing, and review stays blocked. It exits `0` when review is ready and `3` when it isn't, with "rerun init after CI succeeds".

Two things worth pulling out for your repos:

**It never touches the working tree.** The only local write is `.git/info/exclude` — not `.gitignore`, no config files, no workflow files. So it can't collide with the template's sync scripts or pre-commit hooks at all, which retroactively confirms there was nothing for us to set up.

**The review lane needs a required CI check**, and it can only pick from checks that have already succeeded on the default branch. Any repo made from the template has one on day one — `Agent configuration is current` — so `init` will find a candidate instead of leaving review blocked. Worth knowing that the paths filter means it only runs when agent config changes; if you'd rather have a check that runs on every PR to gate the review lane, that's the filter to drop.

**Do we need to set anything up for OpenGSD? No.** It's self-installing on every axis that touches a repo:

- `gsd-core`'s installer writes the commands, agents, workflows, and hooks into whichever runtime you pick, registers the status-line / context-monitor / prompt-guard hooks, and pre-populates Claude Code's `settings.json` permissions.
- `gsd-pi` creates `.gsd/` and adds `gsd.db`, exec output, and `.gsd-worktrees/` to `.gitignore` itself.
- `gsd-loop`'s `init` does the repo-side work — labels, review readiness, required CI check — from the CLI.
- `gsd-browser` and `gsd-graph` are global installs with their own MCP registration.

Two places this template's machinery could get in GSD's way. Neither needs pre-emptive work — just know the fix if you hit it:

1. `sync-mcp.sh` owns `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.codex/config.toml`, and the `mcpServers`/`enabledMcpjsonServers` keys. If a GSD installer writes an MCP entry straight into one of those, CI flags it stale and the next sync reverts it. Move that entry into `.agents/mcp/servers.json` and re-sync. Note the sync only rewrites its one key per file, so GSD's permission additions to `.claude/settings.json` survive untouched.
2. A local-scope `gsd-core` install drops files into `.claude/` and `.cursor/`. `link-skills.sh` only touches names that exist in `.agents/skills`, so GSD's files are safe; at worst pre-commit nags you to `git add` something it left in a skills dir.

The one genuinely repo-side thing GSD can't do for you is `agent_skills` in `.planning/config.json` — pointing it at `.agents/skills/ponytail` makes GSD's subagents inherit this repo's skills. That file doesn't exist until `/gsd-new-project` creates it, so there's nothing to ship; it's a one-line edit afterward if you want it.

Read the site, the docs index (`llms.txt`, 55 pages), the install/planning-artifacts/integrations/project-structure/MCP-setup pages, all 13 repos in the `open-gsd` org, and the npm registry. Pushed, CI green.

**Wired in**

- `gsd-browser` registered in `.agents/mcp/servers.json` → renders into all five adapters. Exact form from the docs: `{"command": "gsd-browser", "args": ["mcp"]}`.
- `AGENTS.md` gets an `Open GSD` section: the five-step phase loop, per-runtime command prefixes (`/gsd-*` for Claude Code/Copilot/OpenCode/Kilo, `/gsd:*` for Gemini CLI, `$gsd-*` for Codex ≥ 0.130.0), where state lives, and install lines for core/pi/browser/loop.
- The best find — GSD Core's `agent_skills` in `.planning/config.json` takes project-root-relative directories containing a `SKILL.md`. That's exactly what `.agents/skills/<name>/` is, so this repo's canonical skills feed GSD's subagents directly: `{"gsd-executor": [".agents/skills/ponytail"]}`.
- `.gitignore`: `.gsd-worktrees/` and `gsd-local-patches/`. `.planning/` and `.gsd/` stay tracked; `gsd.db` was already covered by `*.db`.

**Deliberately not done** — each because the docs said so, not because I guessed:

- **Didn't vendor the five `gsd-loop-*` skills**, even though that repo ships them in `.agents/skills/` in our exact convention. Their `SKILL.md` resolves `playbook.md` and `scripts/*.mjs` *beside itself*, bundled at install time, and the installer's canonical home is `~/.agents/skills/`. Copying the repo's tree would give you skills that fail at runtime. Documented `npx @opengsd/gsd-loop@latest install` then `init` instead.
- **Didn't copy any gsd-core command or agent files** — the install doc is explicit that the installer applies runtime-specific transformations and you must not copy them directly.
- **Didn't hand-write a gsd-graph MCP entry** — it self-registers via `gsd-graph mcp install`. Say the word if you want it, but that's also why AGENTS.md now warns that any installer writing straight into `.mcp.json` gets reverted by the next sync; the entry has to go in the canonical file.
- **No `tools` allowlist on gsd-browser** — 50+ tools and no verified list, so I won't invent names.
- **No installer calls in `bootstrap.sh`** — GSD installs are global and interactive.

**Worth knowing:** the site's version table is stale — npm has gsd-core **1.10.0** (site says 1.9.0), pi 1.15.0, browser 0.2.2, loop 0.4.1, graph 0.4.0. Nothing here pins versions, so it only matters for your reading. Also, GSD Pi's binary is `gsd`, not `gsd-pi` (that name is the installer), and its MCP mode is `gsd --mode mcp`. The homepage's Discover→Spec→Build→Review framing is gsd-loop's four playbooks, not gsd-core's phase loop — AGENTS.md documents the latter.

One thing I could not verify: the docs never state whether `.planning/` should be committed (Pi's `.gsd/` is explicit — `git.commit_docs: true` by default). I made the template track it so plan history is reviewable, and worded that as the repo's choice rather than GSD doctrine. Easy to flip if you know otherwise.

Added as a `Documentation` section in [AGENTS.md](https://github.com/GoatInAHat/template/blob/main/AGENTS.md) — pushed, CI green.

- **README**: write it once the project can be described honestly (what it is, how to run it, how to test it), minimal — no feature tour, no roadmap, no badges — and explicitly *no placeholder* before then. Update it in the same change that makes it wrong, not later.
- **AGENTS.md**: keep current as the project changes, and keep it small. The rule states the reason so it self-enforces: it loads into every agent's context every session, so it records only what changes behaviour, drops anything the code or `--help` already says, and prefers one precise line to a paragraph.

The "no placeholder README" clause also keeps the template consistent with itself — a fresh clone has nothing to describe, so it correctly stays README-less until there's a project there.

AGENTS.md is 107 lines / ~800 words across seven sections, which is still cheap to load every session. If it drifts past roughly double that, the right move is pushing detail into a skill under `.agents/skills/` and leaving a one-line pointer.

**Instructions** — `AGENTS.md` now has a `Dispatching work` section: balance models across intelligence and speed for *any* worker (workflows, subagents, background tasks, scheduled jobs, fan-out), fast tier for mechanical work, strongest for design/review/synthesis. Code quality got the anti-overengineering pass: complete means every path the request needs, not extra paths; never a second implementation of what the repo already does; machinery stays central with thin callers; no abstraction with one implementation and no second caller in sight.

**The devcontainer question — no, it works out of the box.** `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` is `FROM mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu`, a working default; nothing to configure, and the image is one line to swap.

Worth correcting the premise, though: github/docs *does* pin — by digest, in the Dockerfile (`javascript-node:dev-24-bullseye@sha256:3502f1…`). What's absent is an inline `image` in devcontainer.json. The pin lives one file over because that's where they can add build args, extra layers, and a Dependabot-updatable digest. The one real cost of the Dockerfile form is slower Codespaces cold start without prebuilds. If you'd rather have one file than two, inline `"image": "mcr.microsoft.com/devcontainers/base:ubuntu"` and delete the Dockerfile — say the word. I'd keep it, since any project adding apt packages needs the Dockerfile anyway.

**Dependabot — dealt with, and you were right to flag it.** It had already run five `dynamic` jobs and opened PR #1 within minutes of the push. On github.com those update jobs execute on Actions runners, so in a *private* repo made from this template they'd draw down the minutes quota (public repos are free), and each PR then triggers the workflow on top. Config deleted, PR closed, branch deleted. Its one suggestion was legitimate — `actions/checkout@v7.0.1` is current — so I applied that directly instead.

The workflow also now only fires on agent-config paths, so ordinary PRs in a consumer repo cost nothing. There's a comment warning to drop the filters before making it a required status check, since a filtered workflow never reports on the PRs it skips.

**Your three asks**

- `devcontainer.json` → `"name": "devcontainer"`, and no inline image. It builds from `.devcontainer/Dockerfile` the way github/docs does, so the base image is a one-line swap per project instead of a template decision. `github-cli` and `python` features stay (bootstrap needs python3).
- Skills vendored and content-hash locked: `ponytail` + `ponytail-audit`/`-debt`/`-gain`/`-help`/`-review`, and `find-skills`. `AGENTS.md` declares ponytail always on at `full` — which is the skill's own documented default, so no override is fighting upstream.
- Context7 registered by default. One canonical entry now renders to all four harnesses, and it doubles as the live demo of the `tools` allowlist.

Its tools are `resolve-library-id` and **`query-docs`** — Upstash renamed the second one from `get-library-docs`, so the allowlist reflects the current API, not the older name. Config is the remote HTTP endpoint with no credential in git; it works unauthenticated at a lower rate limit, and `CONTEXT7_API_KEY` is documented in `.env.example` for anyone who wants the header.

**Adopted from github/docs**

- Dockerfile-based devcontainer, as above.
- `.github/dependabot.yml` — grouped weekly updates for actions, devcontainer features, and the base image. Their `.gitattributes` lesson too: `* text=auto eol=lf`, which matters here because a CRLF checkout would corrupt the symlinks and scripts.
- `.github/copilot-instructions.md` pointing at `AGENTS.md` — same trick as `CLAUDE.md`, making Copilot a fifth harness for free. Their `.github/instructions/*.instructions.md` (with `applyTo` globs) is the Copilot twin of Cursor's MDC rules, so `.agents/AGENTS.md` now names both as agent-specific config that stays put.

Those are per-project governance, and the last two are language-specific.

One thing worth knowing: I seeded `skills-lock.json` with beer-plan's recorded hashes and my Python checker validated all seven without drift — so it reproduces that repo's JS `computeSkillFolderHash` exactly, and locks written by either tool stay interchangeable.

Rebuilt and pushed: https://github.com/GoatInAHat/template — public, now flagged as a GitHub template repo. CI is green on a clean checkout, including the bootstrap and pre-commit steps.

**One canonical source per category** (the guide's taxonomy):

| Category | Source | Renders to |
|---|---|---|
| Portable | `.agents/skills/<name>/` | `.claude/skills/*`, `.cursor/skills/*` symlinks |
| Generated | `.agents/mcp/servers.json` | `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.codex/config.toml`, `.gemini/settings.json`, `enabledMcpjsonServers` |
| Agent-specific | stays put | `.claude/settings.json` hooks, `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` |

**From `beer`:** `.agents/` layout and self-management docs, `link-skills.sh` (prune + non-symlink guard), `sync-mcp.sh` with `install-codex`, pre-commit + Actions enforcement, `.editorconfig` vendored-skills exception.

**From `beer-plan`:** Gemini as a fourth target (`context.fileName: [AGENTS.md, GEMINI.md]`, so no `GEMINI.md` file needed), `.codex/environments/environment.toml`, the `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE` gate on the session hook (beer re-bootstrapped every local session), per-tool allowlists, and skills-lock hash verification.

**Extended past both:**
- `tools` on a canonical server is now a read-only allowlist → `enabled_tools` (Codex) / `includeTools` (Gemini); Claude and Cursor have no equivalent and get the full surface.
- Sync rewrites *only* `enabledMcpjsonServers` and `mcpServers` in the two hand-owned settings files — without that, Claude Code silently ignores project MCP servers you add.
- `check-skills.py` ports beer-plan's validator to stdlib Python (no npm): folder-hash drift, `name` matching its directory, non-empty description, lock ↔ disk parity. `--update` re-locks, and pre-commit runs it so it isn't manual.
- `.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` for Codespaces — in neither repo, but you named it. All five environments call the same `bootstrap.sh`; only the hook differs.

Verified end to end with a real skill and two MCP servers before resetting to empty: symlinks, all five adapters, hash-drift detection (exit 1), prune on removal.

Left out, say the word on any: `.agents/skills-local/` (both repos ship it dead — beer never links it, and linking it would make pre-commit demand you commit machine-local links); beer-plan's `requirements.json` npm/Neo4j pin machinery; the ponytail-ultra default from beer's AGENTS.md, since the skill isn't vendored in the template and the instruction would dangle. `.codex/environments/environment.toml` is static rather than generated — Codex's own UI rewrites that file, and a generated one would fight it in CI.
